titre: Maury (1851): Wind Charts in Exchange for Logbooks
accroche: Maury gave his charts to anyone who returned logbooks to him. In 1848, a Baltimore ship crosses the Line in 24 days instead of 41.
contenu_vulgarise:
In February 1848, the bark W. H. D. C. Wright, Captain Jackson, of Baltimore, leaves Hampton Roads for Rio de Janeiro. She crosses the equator after 24 days, at 31° west. According to Matthew Fontaine Maury, the usual time to the Line was 41 days. The round trip with Rio takes 75 days. Maury did not sail with her: the route she followed, he had deduced from books.

## A Route Drawn From Statistics

Since 1844, Maury has headed the US Navy's Depot of Charts and Instruments, which will become the Naval Observatory. There he uses ship logbooks to draw up charts of winds and currents. In the third edition of his *Explanations and Sailing Directions*, in 1851, he gives an example. In a square of 5 degrees, he had gathered the records of 700 ships for the month of August. Ships heading south or south-southwest, as the usual route did, met a headwind in 600 of those records. There was no point, he writes, in sending a ship to try: the experience of 700 ships was enough. He recommended crossing the equator no farther east than 30° west, according to Wikipedia.

## Charts Against Logbooks

The Navy's archives were not enough: they were thin above all away from the routes of warships. At the end of 1842, the Navy orders a model “abstract log” to be filled in in a common format, and a version is prepared for the merchant marine. Maury did not sell his charts: he gave them to those who sent him back these logs filled in. Jackson's voyage, widely publicized, increased the demand for charts, and therefore the flow of logs. In 1851, Maury writes that more than a thousand navigators are collecting observations everywhere, without pay, and that such an army of observers had never existed.

In the same text, he also complains of captains who take his results for personal theories. They are, he writes in essence, only the sum of the experience of thousands of navigators, and he specifies that he never promised a route without contrary winds. Some captains abandoned the new route as soon as a headwind arose, then blamed him for a slow crossing.

## From Washington to Brussels

The method went beyond the United States. From August 23 to September 8, 1853, Maury represents his country at the international maritime meteorological conference in Brussels. The final vote, unanimous, adopts a common logbook system: voluntary for merchant ships, mandatory for the ships of the participating navies, according to Wikipedia.

## What This Changes

Maury is often remembered as the man who supposedly “found” the routes. His own description is more modest, and sturdier: wind frequencies by 5-degree square and by month, drawn from what others had noted down. Jackson's figure, for its part, comes from Maury, who was arguing for his method: three crossings, 30 days on average to the Line against 41. What remains to be seen is what three crossings prove, and what a thousand logbooks might have corrected.

repere.texte: In a 5-degree square of latitude and longitude, for the month of August, 700 ship records: 600 gave a headwind for a heading south or south-southwest, that of the usual route to Rio.
repere.source: M. F. Maury, Explanations and Sailing Directions to Accompany the Wind and Current Charts, 3rd ed., Washington, 1851

carte.punch: 700 ships, 600 headwinds: Maury charted his route with statistics.
carte.idee: In 1848, a Baltimore ship crosses the Line in 24 days instead of 41 on Maury's route. He had deduced it from thousands of logbooks, collected by giving his charts to anyone who returned theirs.

pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The text itself, with the pages on the new route to Rio.

quiz.question: What did Maury base the route he recommended for Rio de Janeiro on?
choix: His own Atlantic crossings as a naval officer
Wind frequencies recorded in thousands of logbooks, by 5-degree square
Depth soundings taken along the ships' route
Thermometer temperature measurements taken along Franklin's route
quiz.explication: Maury used logbooks, first those of the Navy and then those that captains sent back to him in exchange for his charts. They were neither his own crossings, nor soundings, nor temperature measurements made on purpose.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Since the Navy's archives were not enough, how did Maury obtain merchant ships' logbooks?
choix: He bought them from captains at the end of each crossing
He gave his charts to those who sent him back their filled-in logs
He boarded the ships himself to record them directly
He obtained them through a maritime tax voted by Congress
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text says Maury did not sell his charts but gave them to anyone who sent back his filled-in logs; he did not sail on Jackson's ship, whose route he deduced from books.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What do the 700 ship records Maury gathered for a 5-degree square in August show?
choix: That 600 ships heading south or south-southwest met a headwind there
That all 700 ships had followed exactly the same route
That 600 ships had suffered a storm at that very spot
That winds there were favorable nine months out of twelve
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that of 700 August records, 600 gave a headwind to ships aiming for the usual heading south or south-southwest; it mentions neither a storm nor a favorable rate over the year.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What did the international maritime meteorological conference in Brussels adopt unanimously in 1853?
choix: An obligation for all ships, merchant ships included, to adopt Maury's charts
The creation of a naval observatory shared by all participating countries
A free sharing of Maury's charts with every navy in the world
A common logbook system, voluntary for merchant ships and mandatory for the participating navies
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Brussels conference's vote adopts a common logbook system, voluntary for the merchant marine and mandatory for the participating navies, not the adoption of Maury's charts or a shared observatory.
